passage: In her first week at the Pune office, Usha hadn't met half her team. But she already knew things about them. At the coffee machine, a senior said, 'Give it to Imran. He'll have it done by evening.' In the lift, two people groaned about another colleague: 'Don't put him on anything with a deadline.' Usha hadn't worked with either. On Thursday she finally sat with Imran on a small task. She watched him reply to every message within the hour, write down each thing he promised, and send a two-line update before leaving. Nothing dramatic. Just the same small thing, every day. On the bus home Usha thought about her own first week: the email she'd forgotten to answer, the meeting she'd been five minutes late to. Somewhere, someone was already describing her.

qa.q: What did the senior say at the coffee machine?
qa.a: The senior said, 'Give it to Imran. He'll have it done by evening.'

qa.q: What was Usha thinking about on the bus home?
qa.a: She felt uneasy thinking about her own first week, the forgotten email and being late, and realised someone was already describing her too.

qa.q: What small choice could Usha make next week, based on what she saw?
qa.a: She could answer emails within the hour and send short updates like Imran, so her small daily actions build the reputation she wants.

qa.q: How might the colleague people groaned about feel if he knew what was said in the lift?
qa.a: He would likely feel hurt and judged by people who may not even have worked with him, and it would be hard to change the story.

grounding: A new employee hears colleagues pass on who is reliable before she has worked with them and sees that reputations grow from small consistent actions.

passage:
'Lavanya, a word before you pick your shifts.'
'Sure, Sarika.'
'Take Dr Menon's night shifts if you can. She actually explains.'
'I haven't met her yet.'
'Nobody needs to meet her. Ask any intern.'
'And Dr Rao?'
'Nice man. But double-check everything he signs. Twice.'
'Has he done something wrong?'
'Not big. Small things. A missed dose chart, a late handover. Everyone knows.'
'That's... a lot to know about someone I've never seen.'
'Welcome to the hospital. By next month, people will be saying things about you too.'
'Like what?'
'Like whether you finish your notes before handover. Whether you answer the ward phone.'
Lavanya looked down at her clipboard, at the notes she hadn't finished yet. 'Okay. Then I'd better finish these.'
Sarika laughed. 'See? You're learning faster than Rao.'

qa.q: Whose night shifts does Sarika tell Lavanya to take?
qa.a: Sarika tells her to take Dr Menon's night shifts because she actually explains.

qa.q: What did Lavanya realise when she looked at her unfinished notes?
qa.a: She realised that people would soon judge her by small things like finishing notes before handover, just as they judged Dr Rao.

qa.q: What choice did Lavanya make after the conversation, and why does it matter?
qa.a: She decided to finish her notes, because small, consistent habits like that are what the ward will remember and pass on about her.

qa.q: How might Dr Rao feel if he knew what interns were told about him?
qa.a: He might feel upset or unfairly labelled, since his reputation came from small slips and was spread before new interns ever met him.

grounding: A new hospital intern hears a senior pass on who is reliable before she meets them and realises reputations come from small, repeated actions shared informally.

passage: Before I met Chinmay, I already knew three things about him. My name's Hafsa, and I had just joined the architecture firm as a junior. On my first day, the office manager said, 'If you're stuck, ask Chinmay, he never says he'll do something and forgets.' The receptionist said his drawings always arrived on time. And in the pantry, someone said a different colleague 'means well but you have to chase him'. It was strange. I hadn't worked with any of them. By the time I did work with Chinmay, a month later, he was exactly as described: small promises, all kept. What stayed with me was how quietly it had all travelled. Nobody sent a memo. It just moved from person to person over tea. So now I reply the same day, even if it's just 'got it, will send by Friday.' I know someone is passing me on.

qa.q: What did the receptionist say about Chinmay?
qa.a: The receptionist said his drawings always arrived on time.

qa.q: Why did Hafsa find it strange to know so much about colleagues already?
qa.a: Hafsa felt surprised to know so much before working with any of them, and was struck by how quietly it had all travelled over tea.

qa.q: What change did Hafsa make after seeing how reputations move, and why?
qa.a: Hafsa now replies the same day, even with a short 'got it', knowing that small kept promises are what people pass on.

qa.q: How might the colleague who 'means well but you have to chase him' be affected by this talk?
qa.a: He may find that new juniors already expect to chase him, which makes it harder to be seen fresh even if he tries to change.

grounding: A junior architect learns about colleagues' reliability through office talk before working with them and realises reputation spreads informally from small kept promises.

passage:
Vice-principal's note, staff induction, week two.
Gopika, our new chemistry teacher, asked me today how everyone already seems to "know" each other. She told me what she has overheard in the staff room: "Karthik will always cover your period if you're ill." "Don't lend the lab key to Mr Rao, you'll never see it again." "Ask Beena, she answers emails the same day." Gopika has not worked with any of them yet, but she has already chosen Karthik for the joint science fair. I said such names are built from years of small, repeated things: returned keys, covered classes, quick replies. She was quiet, then said, "So they're already deciding what I am, too." I told her yes, and that the first month counts. I have paired her with Karthik for the fair and will review how it goes.

qa.q: Whom did Gopika choose for the joint science fair?
qa.a: Karthik.

qa.q: What did Gopika realise when she said, "So they're already deciding what I am, too"?
qa.a: She realised her own reputation is being formed right now, from the same small, repeated actions she has been hearing about in others.

qa.q: What small habits could help Gopika in her first month?
qa.a: Returning borrowed things, answering emails promptly and covering for others when she can, the same kinds of actions that built Karthik's and Beena's names.

qa.q: How might Mr Rao be affected by the staff-room talk?
qa.a: New staff like Gopika decide not to lend him the lab key before ever working with him, so the story shapes his chances whether or not it is still fair.

grounding: A supervisor sees a new teacher absorb colleagues' talk about who is reliable and realise that reputation is built from small consistent actions and passed on informally.

passage:
Monday, week one
Three people have already told me about Anand, and I haven't even met him. At the printer: "If Anand says Friday, it's Thursday." At lunch: "Anand covered my client call when my kid was sick, no questions." And from Maya, rolling her eyes: "Don't depend on Deven, he'll forget." I've never seen Deven forget anything. I've seen Deven twice.
It's strange. I'm already ready to walk into Anand's cabin with more trust than into Deven's, and neither has done a thing for me.
Also a bit scary. Somebody is probably writing a sentence about me at the printer right now. Today I said I'd send the summary by five, and I sent it at 4:40. Small. But I think that's how the sentences get written.
Baljeet

qa.q: What did someone at the printer say about Anand?
qa.a: "If Anand says Friday, it's Thursday."

qa.q: Why does Baljeet feel uneasy about trusting Anand more than Deven?
qa.a: Baljeet notices the trust comes from other people's stories, not from anything either colleague has done for Baljeet, which feels strange and a little unfair.

qa.q: What choice did Baljeet make with the summary, and why does it matter?
qa.a: Sending it at 4:40 instead of five; small kept promises like this are exactly how a reputation gets written.

qa.q: How might Deven be affected by Maya's comment?
qa.a: New people like Baljeet may treat Deven as forgetful before ever working together, whether or not that is fair.

grounding: A new employee hears colleagues describe who is reliable before working with them, and realises that reputation is built from small consistent actions and passed on informally.
